structure.title: Chapters 1–4 · Through the hall of doors
structure.text: Alice follows a rabbit who worries about being late and lands somewhere a key, a door and a body never seem to be the right sizes at the same time. Each solution introduces a fresh practical difficulty. She tries applying school lessons while her own measurements refuse to hold still.

structure.title: Chapters 5–7 · Calls, questions and a tea party
structure.text: A caterpillar demands an identity, a duchess runs a disorderly household and the guests at a tea table refuse to provide a sensible beginning to a conversation. Alice keeps encountering the expectation that a well-brought-up child should know a rule her hosts have just invented.

structure.title: Chapters 8–12 · A croquet match becomes a court case
structure.text: Living mallets and balls prove unreliable sporting equipment. In court the authorities treat evidence with much the same flexibility. The child who began by worrying about her manners acquires some definite opinions about the qualifications of those giving orders.

people.name: Alice
people.role: Visitor with a good memory for rules
people.text: She can remember how a lesson ought to sound even when the words come out wrong. Her attempts to be civil include telling a mouse about her cat. Occasionally the local creatures have excellent grounds for objecting to an impeccably polite child.

people.name: The Cheshire Cat
people.text: Of all the animals Alice encounters, the Cat seems unusually willing to explain the neighbourhood. It can also leave a conversation one body part at a time. The people who insist upon punishing it have trouble specifying exactly what remains within their jurisdiction.

context.title: Lessons that sound almost right
context.text: Alice recites pieces that would once have been familiar in the classroom. Carroll supplies distorted versions where the rhythm remains respectable and the moral has gone wonderfully astray. The sound of a child trying to earn approval survives even if the earlier poems are unfamiliar.

notice.why: At the tea table a minor adjustment to the order of words can make an everyday sentence absurd. The people administering the grammar lesson promptly exempt their own conduct from the demand to make sense.

notice.text: Keep the animals' bodies in the picture.
notice.why: A flamingo has a neck with ideas of its own and a hedgehog can walk away. Alice's game keeps collapsing because the equipment has interests quite independent of the players' wish to finish a shot.

opening: Alice follows a rabbit and finds a world where everyone is ready to correct her, although their rules change whenever she tries to obey them. Her body will not keep a sensible size, conversations turn into traps, and authority becomes more confident as it becomes less reasonable. Carroll gives childhood's experience of being instructed by baffling adults the precision of a logical nightmare. Alice's effort to remain polite and make sense of things supplies the comedy, until politeness starts to look like an unnecessary concession.
